t: Sum of Unique Elements - Count First, Decide Second
o: Sum the values that occur exactly once in nums. In [1,2,3,2] the once-only values are 1 and 3, giving 4; [1,1,1,1,1] contains no unique value so the answer is 0; [1,2,3,4,5] yields 15. Constraints are tiny - at most 100 elements with values at most 100 - so any counting strategy clears the limits with room to spare. The real exercise is doing it cleanly: either count in one pass and aggregate in a second, or maintain the running answer directly by crediting a value on first sight and revoking it on second sight.
k: 'Exactly once' is a frequency property, so the natural shape is count-then-filter.
A single pass suffices if you repair as you go: add a value when its count becomes 1, subtract it when the count becomes 2, ignore every sighting after that.

a.i: Tally every value in a dictionary, then walk the tally and sum the keys whose count equals exactly one. Two simple passes with O(n) extra memory, and the same skeleton answers any exactly-k-times variant.
s: Count occurrences of each value in a hash map.
Iterate over the map and accumulate keys whose count is 1.
Return the accumulated sum (0 when there are none).
a.t: O(n) - one counting pass plus a pass over at most min(n, 100) distinct keys.

a.n: Approach 2: One-Pass Credit/Debit on a Fixed Array
a.i: Because values are bounded by 100, a 101-slot array tracks counts inline. On first occurrence add the value to the answer; on second occurrence subtract it, restoring neutrality; later occurrences change nothing. When the scan ends the answer is already correct - no aggregation pass is needed.
s: Initialize cnt as an array of 101 zeros and ans = 0.
For each x: increment cnt[x]; if it became 1, add x to ans; else if it became 2, subtract x.
a.t: O(n) - a single scan with O(1) work per element.

w: Lead with the one-pass version; the credit/debit idiom is what interviewers want to see. Watch the transition points: adjustments happen only when a count *becomes* 1 or 2, not on every sighting. Pitfalls: summing values with count >= 1 instead of exactly 1; assuming overflow is impossible without checking (true here since n <= 100 and values <= 100 bound the total by 10^4, but worth stating if constraints grow); and using a hash map where a fixed array suffices. Follow-ups: return the sorted multiset of unique elements, generalize to exactly-k-times sums, or process the array as a stream with O(1) memory per distinct value.
